# 19.7 Instrumental Variables and Generalized Method of Moments Estimation



This section provides an introduction to the theory of instrumental variables (IV) estimation and the asymptotic distribution of IV estimators. It is assumed throughout that the IV regression assumptions in Key Concepts 12.3 and 12.4 hold and, moreover, that the instruments are strong. These assumptions apply to cross-sectional data with i.i.d. observations. Under certain conditions, the results derived in this section are applicable to time series data as well, and the extension to time series data is briefly discussed at the end of this section. All asymptotic results in this section are developed under the assumption of strong instruments.

This section begins by presenting the IV regression model and the two stage least squares (TSLS) estimator and its asymptotic distribution in the general case of heteroskedasticity, all in matrix form. It is next shown that, in the special case of homoskedasticity, the TSLS estimator is asymptotically efficient among the class of IV estimators in which the instruments are linear combinations of the exogenous variables. Moreover, the `J`-statistic has an asymptotic chi-squared distribution in which the degrees of freedom equals the number of overidentifying restrictions. This section concludes with a discussion of efficient IV estimation and the test of overidentifying restrictions when the errors are heteroskedastic—a situation in which the efficient IV estimator is known as the efficient generalized method of moments (GMM) estimator \[Hansen (1983)\].





# The IV Estimator in Matrix Form



In this section, we let **`X`** denote the $n \times \left( {k + r + 1} \right)$ matrix of the regressors in the equation of interest, so **`X`** contains the included endogenous regressors (the `X`’s in Key Concept 12.1) *and* the included exogenous regressors (the `W`’s in Key Concept 12.1). That is, in the notation of Key Concept 12.1, the `i`th row of **`X`** is $\mathbf{X}_{i}^{'} = (1\,\,\, X_{1i}\,\,\,\, X_{2i}\,\,\cdots\, X_{ki}\,\,\, W_{1i}\,\,\, W_{2i}\,\cdots\, W_{ri})$. Also, let **`Z`** denote the $n \times (m + r + 1)$ matrix of all the exogenous regressors, both those included in the equation of interest (the `W`’s) *and* those excluded from the equation of interest (the instruments). That is, in the notation of Key Concept 12.1, the `i`th row of **`Z`** is $\mathbf{Z}_{i}^{'} = (1\,\,\, Z_{1i}\,\,\, Z_{2i}\cdots Z_{mi}\,\, W_{1i}\,\,\, W_{2i}\,\cdots\,\,\, W_{ri})$.

With this notation, the IV regression model of Key Concept 12.1, written in matrix form, is



$$\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{U},$$ (19.45)



where **`U`** is the $n \times 1$ vector of errors in the equation of interest, with `i`th element `u``i`.

The matrix **`Z`** consists of all the exogenous regressors, so under the IV regression assumptions in Key Concept 12.4,



$$E\left( {\mathbf{Z}_{i}u_{i}} \right) = 0\quad\left( \text{instrument~exogeneity).} \right.$$ (19.46)



Because there are `k` included endogenous regressors, the first stage regression consists of `k` equations.





# The TSLS estimator



The TSLS estimator is the instrumental variables estimator in which the instruments are the predicted values of **`X`** based on OLS estimation of the first-stage regression. Let $\hat{\mathbf{X}}$ denote this matrix of predicted values, so that the `i`th row of $\hat{\mathbf{X}}$ is $({\hat{X}}_{1i}\,\,\,{\hat{X}}_{2i}\,\,\cdots\,\,\,{\hat{X}}_{ki}\,\,\, W_{1i}\cdots\,\,\, W_{ri})$, where ${\hat{X}}_{1i}$ is the predicted value from the regression of `X`1`i` on **`Z`** and so forth. Because the `W`’s are contained in **`Z`**, the predicted value from a regression of `W`1`i` on **`Z`** is just `W`1`i` and so forth, so $\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X}$, where $\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}} = \mathbf{Z}\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\,\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Z}\prime$ \[see Equation (19.27)\]. Accordingly, the TSLS estimator is



$${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{TSLS} = {(\hat{\mathbf{X}}'\,\hat{\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\,\hat{\mathbf{X}}'\,\mathbf{Y}.$$ (19.47)



Because $\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X},\hat{\mathbf{X}}\prime\,\hat{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{X}\prime\mspace{2mu}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{X}}\prime\,\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\prime\mspace{2mu}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Y}$, the TSLS estimator can be rewritten as



$${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{TSLS} = \left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mspace{2mu}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mspace{2mu}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Y}.$$ (19.48)











# Asymptotic Distribution of the TSLS Estimator



Substituting Equation (19.45) into Equation (19.48), rearranging, and multiplying by $\sqrt{n}$ yields the expression for the centered and scaled TSLS estimator:



$$\begin{array}{lll}
{\sqrt{n}({\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{TSLS} - \mathbf{\beta})} & = & {\left( \frac{\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X}}{n} \right)^{- 1}\,\frac{\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{U}}{\sqrt{n}}} \\
 & = & {\left\lbrack {\frac{\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Z}}{n}\left( \frac{\mathbf{Z}'\mathbf{Z}}{n} \right)^{- 1}\frac{\mathbf{Z}'\mathbf{X}}{n}} \right\rbrack^{- 1}\,\left\lbrack {\frac{\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Z}}{n}\left( \frac{\mathbf{Z}'\mathbf{Z}}{n} \right)^{- 1}\,\frac{\mathbf{Z}'\mathbf{U}}{\sqrt{n}}} \right\rbrack,}
\end{array}$$ (19.49)



where the second equality uses the definition of **`P``Z`**. Under the IV regression assumptions, $\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}$ and $\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}$, where $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}} = E\left( {\mathbf{X}_{i}\mathbf{Z}\prime_{i}} \right)$ and $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}} = E\left( {\mathbf{Z}_{i}\mathbf{Z}\prime_{i}} \right)$. In addition, under the IV regression assumptions, $\mathbf{Z}_{i}u_{i}$ is i.i.d. with mean 0 \[Equation (19.46)\] and a positive definite covariance matrix, so its sum, divided by $\sqrt{n}$, satisfies the conditions of the multivariate central limit theorem (Key Concept 19.2) and



$$\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{U}/\sqrt{n}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\mathbf{\Psi}_{ZU},\text{~where~}\mathbf{\Psi}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{U}}\ \text{∼}N\left( {0,\ \mathbf{H}\,} \right),\ \mathbf{H} = E\left( {\mathbf{Z}_{i}\mathbf{Z}\prime_{i\ }u_{i}^{2}} \right)$$ (19.50)



and ${}_{}\mathbf{\Psi}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{U}}$ is $\left( {m + r + 1} \right) \times 1.$

Application of Equation (19.50) and of the limits $\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}$ and $\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}$ to Equation (19.49) yields the result that, under the IV regression assumptions, the TSLS estimator is asymptotically normally distributed:



$$\sqrt{n}\ \left( {{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{TSLS} - \mathbf{\beta}} \right)\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}\Psi_{\mathbf{Z}U}\ \sim \ N{\left( {0\text{,~}\textbf{Σ}^{TSLS}} \right),}$$ (19.51)



where



$$\textbf{Σ}^{TSLS} = \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}\ }^{- 1}H\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}\ }^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}\ }\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1},$$ (19.52)



where **`H`** is defined in Equation (19.50).





# Standard errors for TSLS



The formula in Equation (19.52) is daunting. Nevertheless, it provides a way to estimate $\textbf{Σ}^{TSLS}$ by substituting sample moments for the population moments. The resulting variance estimator is



$${\hat{\textbf{Σ}}}^{TSLS} = {({\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}^{- 1}{}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\hat{H}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}\,{({\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1},$$ (19.53)



where ${\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}} = \mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}\,/\, n,{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}} = \mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}\,/\, n,{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{X}\text{/}n$, and



$$\hat{\mathbf{H}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\mathbf{Z}_{i}\mspace{2mu}\mathbf{Z}_{i}\,{\hat{u}}_{i}^{2},\text{~where~}\hat{\mathbf{U}} = \mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{TSLS},$$ (19.54)



so that $\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ is the vector of TSLS residuals, and where ${\hat{u}}_{i}$ is the `i`th element of that vector (the TSLS residual for the `i`th observation).

The TSLS standard errors are the square roots of the diagonal elements of ${\hat{\textbf{Σ}}}^{{TSLS}/n}$.









# Properties of TSLS When the Errors Are Homoskedastic



If the errors are homoskedastic, then the TSLS estimator is asymptotically efficient among the class of IV estimators in which the instruments are linear combinations of the rows of **`Z`**. This result is the IV counterpart to the Gauss–Markov theorem and constitutes an important justification for using TSLS.





# The TSLS distribution under homoskedasticity



If the errors are homoskedastic—that is, if $E\left( {u_{i}^{2}|\mathbf{Z}_{i}} \right) = \sigma_{u}^{2}$—then $\mathbf{H} = E\left( {\mathbf{Z}_{i}\mathbf{Z}\prime_{i\ }u_{i}^{2}} \right) = E\left\lbrack {E\left( {\mathbf{Z}_{i}\mathbf{Z}\prime_{i\ }u_{i}{}^{2}|\mathbf{Z}_{i}} \right)} \right\rbrack = E\left\lbrack {\mathbf{Z}_{i}\mathbf{Z}\prime_{i}E\left( {u_{i}{}^{2}|\mathbf{Z}_{i}} \right)} \right\rbrack\ = \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\sigma_{u}^{2}$. In this case, the variance of the asymptotic distribution of the TSLS estimator in Equation (19.52) simplifies to



$$\textbf{Σ}^{TSLS} = \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\sigma_{u}^{2}\ \text{(homoskedasticity only).}$$ (19.55)



The homoskedasticity-only estimator of the TSLS variance matrix is



$$\begin{matrix}
{{\widetilde{\textbf{Σ}}}^{TSLS} = {({\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}{\hat{\mathbf{Q}}}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}{\hat{\sigma}}_{u}^{2} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{U}}'\hat{\mathbf{U}}}{n - k - r - 1}} \\
\text{(homoskedasticity~only),}
\end{matrix}$$ (19.56)



and the homoskedasticity-only TSLS standard errors are the square roots of the diagonal elements of ${\widetilde{\textbf{Σ}}}^{TSLS}/n$.







# The class of IV estimators that use linear combinations of Z



The class of IV estimators that use linear combinations of **`Z`** as instruments can be generated in two equivalent ways. Both start with the same moment equation: Under the assumption of instrument exogeneity, the errors $\mathbf{U} = Y - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta}$ are uncorrelated with the exogenous regressors; that is, at the true value of **`β`**, Equation (19.46) implies that



$$E\left\lbrack {\left( {\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta}} \right)\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right\rbrack = 0.$$ (19.57)



Equation (19.57) constitutes a system of $m + r + 1$ equations involving the $k + r + 1$ unknown elements of $\mathbf{\beta}$. When $m > k$, these equations are redundant in the sense that all are satisfied at the true value of **`β`**. When these population moments are replaced by their sample moments, the system of equations $\left( {\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}} \right)\prime\mathbf{Z} = 0$ can be solved for **`b`** when there is exact identification ($m = k$). This value of **`b`** is the IV estimator of **`β`**. However, when there is overidentification ($m > k$), the equations in the system cannot be simultaneously satisfied by the same value of **`b`** because of sampling variation—there are more equations than unknowns—and, in general, this system does not have a solution.

The first approach to the problem of estimating **`β`** when there is overidentification is to trade off the desire to satisfy each equation by minimizing a quadratic form involving all the equations. Specifically, let **`A`** be an $(m + r + 1) \times (m + r + 1)$ symmetric positive semidefinite weight matrix, and let ${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV}$ denote the estimator that minimizes



$$\text{min}_{b}\left( {\textit{\textbf{Y}} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}} \right)\prime\mathbf{Z}A\mathbf{Z}\prime\left( {\textit{\textbf{Y}} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}}\text{).} \right.$$ (19.58)



The solution to this minimization problem is found by taking the derivative of the objective function with respect to **`b`**, setting the result equal to 0, and rearranging. Doing so yields ${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV}$, the IV estimator based on the weight matrix **`A`**:



$${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV} = \left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z}\prime\textit{\textbf{Y}}.$$ (19.59)



Comparison of Equations (19.59) and (19.48) shows that the TSLS estimator is the IV estimator with $\textit{\textbf{A}} = \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1}$. That is, TSLS is the solution of the minimization problem in Equation (19.58) with $\textit{\textbf{A}} = \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1}$.

The calculations leading to Equations (19.51) and (19.52), applied to ${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}_{\textit{\textbf{A}}}^{IV}$, show that



$$\begin{matrix}
{\sqrt{n}({\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}_{\textit{\textbf{A}}}^{IV} - \mathbf{\beta})\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}N(0,\,\textbf{Σ}_{\textit{\textbf{A}}}^{IV}),\,\text{where}} \\
{\textbf{Σ}_{\textit{\textbf{A}}}^{IV} = {(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\textit{\textbf{A}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}{(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\textit{\textbf{A}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}.}
\end{matrix}$$ (19.60)



The second way to generate the class of IV estimators that use linear combinations of **`Z`** is to consider IV estimators in which the instruments are ***ZB***, where **`B`** is an $(m + r + 1) \times (k + r + 1)$ matrix with full column rank. Then the system of $(k + r + 1)$ equations, $\left( {\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}} \right)\prime\mathbf{Z}\textit{\textbf{B}} = 0$, can be solved uniquely for the $(k + r + 1)$ unknown elements of **`b`**. Solving these equations for **`b`** yields ${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{IV} = \left( {\textit{\textbf{B}}\prime\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}\left( {\textit{\textbf{B}}\prime\mathbf{Z}\prime\textit{\textbf{Y}}} \right)$, and substitution of $\textit{\textbf{B}} = \textit{\textbf{A}}\mathbf{Z}\prime\mspace{2mu}\mathbf{X}$ into this expression yields Equation (19.59).

Thus the two approaches to defining IV estimators that are linear combinations of the instruments yield the same family of IV estimators. It is conventional to work with the first approach, in which the IV estimator solves the quadratic minimization problem in Equation (19.58), and that is the approach taken here.







# Asymptotic efficiency of TSLS under homoskedasticity



If the errors are homoskedastic, then $\textit{\textbf{H}} = \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\sigma_{u}^{2}$, and the expression for $\textbf{Σ}_{\textit{\textbf{A}}}^{IV}$ in Equation (19.60) becomes



$$\textbf{Σ}_{\textit{\textbf{A}}}^{IV} = \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\textit{\textbf{A}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\textit{\textbf{A}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\textit{\textbf{A}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}\ }\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\textit{\textbf{A}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\sigma_{u}^{2}.$$ (19.61)



To show that TSLS is asymptotically efficient among the class of estimators that are linear combinations of **`Z`** when the errors are homoskedastic, we need to show that, under homoskedasticity,



$$\mathbf{c}\prime\textbf{Σ}_{\textit{\textbf{A}}}^{IV}c \geq \mathbf{c}\prime\textbf{Σ}^{TSLS}\mathbf{c}$$ (19.62)



for all positive semidefinite matrices **`A`** and all $(k + r + 1) \times 1$ vectors **`c`**, where $\textbf{Σ}^{TSLS} = \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\sigma_{u}^{2}$ \[Equation (19.55)\]. The inequality (19.62), which is proven in Appendix 19.6, is the same efficiency criterion as is used in the multivariate Gauss–Markov theorem in Key Concept 19.3. Consequently, TSLS is the efficient IV estimator under homoskedasticity among the class of estimators in which the instruments are linear combinations of **`Z`**.







# The J-statistic under homoskedasticity



The `J`-statistic (Key Concept 12.6) tests the null hypothesis that all the overidentifying restrictions hold against the alternative that some or all of them do not hold.

The idea of the `J`-statistic is that, if the overidentifying restrictions hold, `u``i` will be uncorrelated with the instruments, and thus a regression of **`U`** on **`Z`** will have population regression coefficients that all equal 0. In practice, **`U`** is not observed, but it can be estimated by the TSLS residuals $\hat{\mathbf{U}}$, so a regression of $\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ on **`Z`** should yield statistically insignificant coefficients. Accordingly, the TSLS `J`-statistic is the homoskedasticity-only `F`-statistic testing the hypothesis that the coefficients on **`Z`** are all 0, in the regression of $\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ on **`Z`**, multiplied by $(m + r + 1)$ so that the `F`-statistic is in its asymptotic chi-squared form.

An explicit formula for the `J`-statistic can be obtained using Equation (7.13) for the homoskedasticity-only `F`-statistic. The unrestricted regression is the regression of $\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ on the $m + r + 1$ regressors **`Z`**, and the restricted regression has no regressors. Thus, in the notation of Equation (7.13), $SSR_{unrestricted} = \hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime M_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}$, and ${SSR_{restricted} = \hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime}\hat{\mathbf{U}}$, so $SSR_{restricted} - SSR_{unrestricted} = \hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime\hat{\mathbf{U}} - \hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime M_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}} = \hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime P_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ and the `J`-statistic is



$$J = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{U}}'P_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}}{\hat{\mathbf{U}}'M_{\mathbf{Z}}{\hat{\mathbf{U}}/{(n - m - r - 1)}}}.$$ (19.63)



The method for computing the `J`-statistic described in Key Concept 12.6 entails testing only the hypothesis that the coefficients on the excluded instruments are 0. Although these two methods have different computational steps, they produce identical `J`-statistics (Exercise 19.14).

It is shown in Appendix 19.6 that, under the null hypothesis that $E(u_{i}\mathbf{Z}_{i}) = 0$,



$$J\ \operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\chi_{m - k}^{2}.$$ (19.64)











# Generalized Method of Moments Estimation in Linear Models



If the errors are heteroskedastic, then the TSLS estimator is no longer efficient among the class of IV estimators that use linear combinations of **`Z`** as instruments. The efficient estimator in this case is known as the efficient generalized method of moments (GMM) estimator. In addition, if the errors are heteroskedastic, then the `J`-statistic as defined in Equation (19.63) no longer has a chi-squared distribution. However, an alternative formulation of the `J`-statistic, constructed using the efficient GMM estimator, does have a chi-squared distribution with $m - k$ degrees of freedom.

These results parallel the results for the estimation of the usual regression model with exogenous regressors and heteroskedastic errors: If the errors are heteroskedastic, then the OLS estimator is not efficient among estimators that are linear in **`Y`** (the Gauss–Markov conditions are not satisfied), and the homoskedasticity-only `F`-statistic no longer has an `F` distribution, even in large samples. In the regression model with exogenous regressors and heteroskedasticity, the efficient estimator is weighted least squares; in the IV regression model with heteroskedasticity, the efficient estimator uses a different weighting matrix than TSLS, and the resulting estimator is the efficient GMM estimator.





# GMM estimation



<a href="#glossary.xhtml#P7001015391000000000000000005778" id="ch19_pg0008.xhtml#P7001015391000000000000000008D7C" class="keyword" data-uri="M19_STOC1991_04_SE_C19.xhtml#P7001015391000000000000000008D7C" data-offlinesupport="yes">Generalized method of moments (GMM)</a> estimation is a general method for the estimation of the parameters of linear or nonlinear models, in which the parameters are chosen to provide the best fit to multiple equations, each of which sets a sample moment to 0. These equations, which in the context of GMM are called moment conditions, typically cannot all be satisfied simultaneously. The GMM estimator trades off the desire to satisfy each of the equations by minimizing a quadratic objective function.

In the linear IV regression model with exogenous variables **`Z`**, the class of GMM estimators consists of all the estimators that are solutions to the quadratic minimization problem in Equation (19.58). Thus the class of GMM estimators based on the full set of instruments **`Z`** with different-weight matrices **`A`** is the same as the class of IV estimators in which the instruments are linear combinations of **`Z`**. In the linear IV regression model, GMM is just another name for the class of estimators we have been studying—that is, estimators that solve Equation (19.58).







# The asymptotically efficient GMM estimator



Among the class of GMM estimators, the efficient GMM estimator is the GMM estimator with the smallest asymptotic variance matrix \[where the smallest variance matrix is defined as in Equation (19.62)\]. Thus the result in Equation (19.62) can be restated as saying that TSLS is the efficient GMM estimator in the linear model when the errors are homoskedastic.

To motivate the expression for the efficient GMM estimator when the errors are heteroskedastic, recall that when the errors are homoskedastic, **`H`** \[the variance matrix of **`Z`**i`u``i`; see Equation (19.50)\] equals $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\sigma_{u}^{2}$, and the asymptotically efficient weight matrix is obtained by setting $\textit{\textbf{A}} = \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1}$, which yields the TSLS estimator. In large samples, using the weight matrix $\textit{\textbf{A}} = \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1}$ is equivalent to using $\textit{\textbf{A}} = \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\sigma_{u}^{2}} \right)^{- 1} = \textit{\textbf{H}}^{- 1}$. This interpretation of the TSLS estimator suggests that, by analogy, the efficient IV estimator under heteroskedasticity can be obtained by setting $\textit{\textbf{A}} = \textit{\textbf{H}}^{- 1}$ and solving



$$\text{min}_{b}\left( {\textit{\textbf{Y}} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}} \right)\prime\mathbf{Z}\textit{\textbf{H}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Z}\prime\left( {\textit{\textbf{Y}} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}}\text{).} \right.$$ (19.65)



This analogy is correct: The solution to the minimization problem in Equation (19.65) is the efficient GMM estimator. Let ${\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$ denote the solution to the minimization problem in Equation (19.65). By Equation (19.59), this estimator is



$${\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM} = \left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}\textit{\textbf{H}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}\textit{\textbf{H}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Z}\prime\textit{\textbf{Y}}.$$ (19.66)



The asymptotic distribution of ${\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$ is obtained by substituting $\textit{\textbf{A}} = \textit{\textbf{H}}^{- 1}$ into Equation (19.60) and simplifying; thus



$$\begin{matrix}
{\sqrt{n}({\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM} - \mathbf{\beta})\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}N(0,\,\textbf{Σ}^{Eff.GMM}),} \\
{\text{where~}\textbf{Σ}^{Eff.GMM} = \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\textit{\textbf{H}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}.}
\end{matrix}$$ (19.67)



The result that ${\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$ is the efficient GMM estimator is proven by showing that $\mathbf{c}\prime\textbf{Σ}_{\textit{\textbf{A}}}^{IV}\mathbf{c} \geq \mathbf{c}\prime\textbf{Σ}^{Eff.GMM}c$ for all vectors **`c`**, where $\textbf{Σ}_{A}^{IV}$ is given in Equation (19.60). The proof of this result is given in Appendix 19.6.







# Feasible efficient GMM estimation



The GMM estimator defined in Equation (19.66) is not a feasible estimator because it depends on the unknown variance matrix **`H`**. However, a feasible efficient GMM estimator can be computed by substituting a consistent estimator of **`H`** into the minimization problem of Equation (19.65) or, equivalently, by substituting a consistent estimator of **`H`** into the formula for ${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$ in Equation (19.66).

The efficient GMM estimator can be computed in two steps. In the first step, estimate **`β`** using any consistent estimator. Use this estimator of **`β`** to compute the residuals from the equation of interest, and then use these residuals to compute an estimator of **`H`**. In the second step, use this estimator of **`H`** to estimate the optimal weight matrix **`H`**<sup>−1</sup> and to compute the efficient GMM estimator. To be concrete, in the linear IV regression model, it is natural to use the TSLS estimator in the first step and to use the TSLS residuals to estimate **`H`**. If TSLS is used in the first step, then the feasible efficient GMM estimator computed in the second step is



$${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM} = \left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}{\hat{\textit{\textbf{H}}}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{X}\,} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}{\hat{\textit{\textbf{H}}}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Z}\prime\textit{\textbf{Y}},$$ (19.68)



where $\hat{\textit{\textbf{H}}}$ is given in Equation (19.54).

Because $\hat{\textit{\textbf{H}}}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\textit{\textbf{H}},\sqrt{n}\,\left( {{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM} - {\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}} \right)\,\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}0$ (Exercise 19.12), and



$$\sqrt{n}\left( {{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM} - \mathbf{\beta}} \right)\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}N\left( {0,\ \textbf{Σ}^{Eff.GMM}} \right)\text{,}$$ (19.69)



where $\textbf{Σ}^{Eff.GMM} = \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\textit{\textbf{H}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}$ \[Equation (19.67)\]. That is, the feasible two-step estimator ${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$ in Equation (19.68) is, asymptotically, the efficient GMM estimator.







# The heteroskedasticity-robust J-statistic



The <a href="#glossary.xhtml#heteroskedasticity-robustJ-statistic" id="ch19_pg0008.xhtml#kt-heteroskedasticity-robustJ-statistic" class="keyword" data-offlinesupport="yes">heteroskedasticity-robust <var>J</var>-statistic</a>, also known as the <a href="#glossary.xhtml#heteroskedasticity-robustJ-statistic" id="ch19_pg0008.xhtml#P7001015391000000000000000008D7F" class="keyword" data-uri="M19_STOC1991_04_SE_C19.xhtml#P7001015391000000000000000008D7F" data-offlinesupport="yes">GMM <var>J</var>-statistic</a>, is the counterpart of the TSLS-based `J`-statistic, computed using the efficient GMM estimator and weight function. That is, the GMM `J`-statistic is given by



$$J^{GMM} = {({\mathbf{Z}\prime{\hat{\mathbf{U}}}^{{}^{GMM}}})}\prime{\hat{\textit{\textbf{H}}}}^{- 1}{({\mathbf{Z}\prime{\hat{\mathbf{U}}}^{{}^{GMM}}})}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n,$$ (19.70)



where ${\hat{\mathbf{U}}}^{GMM} = \textit{\textbf{Y}} - \mathbf{X}{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$ are the residuals from the equation of interest, estimated by (feasible) efficient GMM, and ${\hat{\textit{\textbf{H}}}}^{- 1}$ is the weight matrix used to compute ${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$.

Under the null hypothesis $E{({\mathbf{Z}_{i}u_{i}})} = 0,\ J^{GMM}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\chi_{m - k}^{2}$ (see Appendix 19.6).







# GMM with time series data



The results in this section were derived under the IV regression assumptions for cross–sectional data. In many applications, however, these results extend to time series applications of IV regression and GMM. Although a formal mathematical treatment of GMM with time series data is beyond the scope of this book (for such a treatment, see Hayashi, 2000, Chapter 6), we nevertheless will summarize the key ideas of GMM estimation with time series data. This summary assumes familiarity with the material in Chapters 14 and 16. For this discussion, it is assumed that the variables are stationary.

It is useful to distinguish between two types of applications: applications in which the error term `u``t` is serially correlated and applications in which `u``t` is serially uncorrelated. If the error term `u``t` is serially correlated, then the asymptotic distribution of the GMM estimator continues to be normally distributed, but the formula for **`H`** in Equation (19.50) is no longer correct. Instead, the correct expression for **`H`** depends on the autocovariances of **`Z`**`t``u``t` and is analogous to the formula given in Equation (16.14) for the variance of the OLS estimator when the error term is serially correlated. The efficient GMM estimator is still constructed using a consistent estimator of **`H`**; however, that consistent estimator must be computed using the HAC methods discussed in Chapter 16.

If ***Z**tu*`t` is not serially correlated, then HAC estimation of **`H`** is unnecessary, and the formulas presented in this section all extend to time series GMM applications. In modern applications to finance and macroeconometrics, it is common to encounter models in which the error term represents an unexpected or unforecastable disturbance, in which case the model typically implies that ***Z**tu*`t` is serially uncorrelated. For example, consider a model with a single included endogenous variable and no included exogenous variables so that the equation of interest is $\text{Y}_{t} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}X_{t} + u_{t}$. Suppose that an economic theory implies that `u``t` is unpredictable given past information. Then the theory implies the moment condition



$$E{({u_{t}|\text{Y}_{t - 1},\ X_{t - 1},\ Z_{t - 1},\ \text{Y}_{t - 2},\ X_{t - 2},\ Z_{t - 2},\ \cdots})} = 0,$$ (19.71)



where `Z``t`−1 is the lagged value of some other variable. The moment condition in Equation (19.71) implies that all the lagged variables $\text{Y}_{t - 1},\ X_{t - 1},\ Z_{t - 1},\ \text{Y}_{t - 2},\ X_{t - 2},Z_{t - 2},\ \cdots$ are candidates for being valid instruments (they satisfy the exogeneity condition). Moreover, because $u_{t - 1} = \text{Y}_{t - 1} - \beta_{0} - \beta_{1}X_{t - 1}$, the moment condition in Equation (19.71) is equivalent to $E{({u_{t}\,|u_{t - 1},\ X_{t - 1},\ Z_{t - 1},\ u_{t - 2},\ X_{t - 2},\ Z_{t - 2},\ \cdots})} = 0$. Because `u``t` is serially uncorrelated, HAC estimation of **`H`** is unnecessary. The theory of GMM presented in this section, including efficient GMM estimation and the GMM `J`-statistic, therefore applies directly to time series applications with moment conditions of the form in Equation (19.71), under the hypothesis that the moment condition in Equation (19.71) is, in fact, correct.









<!--?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?-->





# Summary



1.

The linear multiple regression model in matrix form is $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{U}$, where **`Y`** is the $n \times 1$ vector of observations on the dependent variable, **`X`** is the $n \times {({k + 1})}$ matrix of `n` observations on the $k + 1$ regressors (including a constant), **`β`** is the $k + 1$ vector of unknown parameters, and **`U`** is the $n \times 1$ vector of error terms.



2.

The OLS estimator is $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} = {({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Y}$. Under the first four least squares assumptions in Key Concept 19.1, $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}$ is consistent and asymptotically normally distributed. If in addition the errors are homoskedastic, then the conditional variance of $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}$ is var${({\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}\,|\mathbf{X}\,})} = \sigma_{u}^{2}{({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}$.



3.

General linear restrictions on **`β`** can be written as the `q` equations $R\mathbf{\beta} = \mathbf{r}\text{,}$ and this formulation can be used to test joint hypotheses involving multiple coefficients or to construct confidence sets for elements of **`β`**.



4.

When the regression errors are i.i.d. and normally distributed, conditional on **`X`**, $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}$ has an exact normal distribution, and the homoskedasticity-only `t`- and `F`-statistics have exact $t_{n - k - 1}$ and $F_{q,\ n - k - 1}\ $ distributions, respectively.



5.

The Gauss–Markov theorem says that, if the errors are homoskedastic and conditionally uncorrelated across observations and if $E(u_{i}|\mathbf{X}) = 0$, the OLS estimator is efficient among linear conditionally unbiased estimators (that is, OLS is BLUE).



6.

If the error covariance matrix $\textbf{Ω}$ is not proportional to the identity matrix and if $\textbf{Ω}$ is known or can be estimated, then the GLS estimator is asymptotically more efficient than OLS. However, GLS requires that, in general, `u``i` be uncorrelated with *all* observations on the regressors, not just with **`X`**`i`, as is required by OLS, an assumption that must be evaluated carefully in applications.



7.

The TSLS estimator is a member of the class of GMM estimators of the linear model. In GMM, the coefficients are estimated by making the sample covariance between the regression error and the exogenous variables as small as possible—specifically, by solving $\text{min}_{b}\,{\lbrack{{({\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}})}\prime\mathbf{Z}}\rbrack}\mathbf{A}\,{\lbrack{\mathbf{Z}\prime{({\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}})}}\rbrack}$, where **`A`** is a non-random positive definite matrix. The asymptotically efficient GMM estimator sets $\mathbf{A} = {\lbrack{E{({\mathbf{Z}_{i}\mathbf{Z}_{i}\prime u_{i}^{2}})}}\rbrack}^{- 1}$. When the errors are homoskedastic, the asymptotically efficient GMM estimator in the linear IV regression model is TSLS.

# Appendix 19.1 Summary of Matrix Algebra



This appendix summarizes vectors, matrices, and the elements of matrix algebra used in Chapter 19. The purpose of this appendix is to review some concepts and definitions from a course in linear algebra, not to replace such a course.





# Definitions of Vectors and Matrices



A vector is a collection of `n` numbers or elements, collected either in a column (a column vector) or in a row (a row vector). The `n`-dimensional column vector **`b`** and the `n`-dimensional row vector **`c`** are



$$\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix}
b_{1} \\
b_{2} \\
 \vdots \\
b_{n}
\end{bmatrix}\text{~and~}\mathbf{c} = \begin{bmatrix}
c_{1} & c_{2} & \cdots & c_{n}
\end{bmatrix},$$



where `b`<sub>1</sub> is the first element of **`b`** and, in general, `b`<sub>`i`</sub> is the `i`<sup>th</sup> element of **`b`**.

Throughout, a boldface denotes a vector or matrix.

A matrix is a collection, or an array, of numbers or elements, in which the elements are laid out in columns and rows. The dimension of a matrix is $n \times m$, where `n` is the number of rows and `m` is the number of columns. The $n \times m$ matrix **`A`** is



$$\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix}
a_{11} & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1m} \\
a_{21} & a_{22} & \cdots & a_{2m} \\
 \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
a_{n1} & a_{n2} & \cdots & a_{nm}
\end{bmatrix},$$



where *aij* is the (`i`, `j`) element of **`A`**; that is, *aij* is the element that appears in the `i`th row and `j`th column. An $n \times m$ matrix consists of `n` row vectors or, alternatively, of `m` column vectors.

To distinguish one-dimensional numbers from vectors and matrices, a one-dimensional number is called a scalar.







# Types of Matrices







# Square, symmetric, and diagonal matrices



A matrix is said to be square if the number of rows equals the number of columns. A square matrix is said to be symmetric if its (`i`, `j`) element equals its (`j`, `i`) element. A diagonal matrix is a square matrix in which all the off-diagonal elements equal 0; that is, if the square matrix **`A`** is diagonal, then $a_{ij} = 0$ for i ≠ j.







# Special matrices



An important matrix is the identity matrix, `I``n`, which is an $n \times n$ diagonal matrix with 1’s on the diagonal. The null matrix, $0_{n \times m}$, is the $n \times m$ matrix with all elements equal to 0.







# The transpose



The transpose of a matrix switches the rows and the columns. That is, the transpose of a matrix turns the $n \times m$ matrix **`A`** into the $m \times n$ matrix, which is denoted by $\mathbf{A}\prime$, where the (`i`, `j`) element of **`A`** becomes the (`j`, `i`) element of $\mathbf{A}\prime$; said differently, the transpose of the matrix **`A`** turns the rows of **`A`** into the columns of $\mathbf{A}\prime$. If *aij* is the (`i`, `j`) element of **`A`**, then $\mathbf{A}\prime$ (the transpose of **`A`**) is



$$\mathbf{A}' = \begin{bmatrix}
a_{11} & a_{21} & \cdots & a_{n1} \\
a_{12} & a_{22} & \cdots & a_{n2} \\
 \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
a_{1m} & a_{2m} & \cdots & a_{nm}
\end{bmatrix}.$$



The transpose of a vector is a special case of the transpose of a matrix. Thus the transpose of a vector turns a column vector into a row vector; that is, if **`b`** is an $n \times 1$ column vector, then its transpose is the $1 \times n$ row vector:



$$\mathbf{b}\prime = \begin{bmatrix}
b_{1} & b_{2} & \cdots & b_{n}
\end{bmatrix}.$$



The transpose of a row vector is a column vector.









# Elements of Matrix Algebra: Addition and Multiplication







# Matrix addition



Two matrices **`A`** and **`B`** that have the same dimensions (for example, that are both $n \times m$) can be added together. The sum of two matrices is the sum of their elements; that is, if $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$, then $c_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij}$. A special case of matrix addition is vector addition: If **`a`** and **`b`** are both $n \times 1$ column vectors, then their sum, $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$, is the element-wise sum; that is, $c_{i} = a_{i} + b_{i}$.







# Vector and matrix multiplication



Let **`a`** and **`b`** be two $n \times 1$ column vectors. Then the product of the transpose of **`a`** (which is itself a row vector) and **`b`** is $\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{b} = {\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{a_{i}b_{i}}}$. Applying this definition with $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a}$ yields $\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{a} = {\sum_{i = 1}^{n}a_{i}^{2}}$.

Similarly, the matrices **`A`** and **`B`** can be multiplied together if they are conformable—that is, if the number of columns of **`A`** equals the number of rows of **`B`**. Specifically, suppose that **`A`** has dimension $n \times m$ and **`B`** has dimension $m \times r$. Then the product of **`A`** and **`B`** is an $n \times r$ matrix, **`C`**; that is, $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$, where the (`i`, `j`) element of **`C`** is $c_{ij} = {\sum_{k = 1}^{m}{a_{ik}b_{kj}}}$. Said differently, the (`i`, `j`) element of ***AB*** is the product of multiplying the row vector that is the `i`th row of **`A`** by the column vector that is the `j`th column of **`B`**.

The product of a scalar `d` with the matrix **`A`** has the (`i`, `j`) element *da<sub>ij</sub>*; that is, each element of **`A`** is multiplied by the scalar `d`.







# Some useful properties of matrix addition and multiplication



Let **`A`** and **`B`** be matrices. Then

1.

$\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{A}$;



2.

$\left( {\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}} \right) + \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A} + \left( {\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{C}} \right)$;



3.

$\left( {\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}} \right)\prime = \mathbf{A}\prime + \mathbf{B}\prime$;



4.

If $\mathbf{A}$ is $n \times m$, then $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{I}_{m} = \mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{I}_{n}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}$;



5.

$\mathbf{A}\left( {\mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}} \right) = \left( {\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}} \right)\mathbf{C}$;



6.

$\left( {\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}} \right)\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{C} + \mathbf{B}\mathbf{C}$; and



7.

$\left( {\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}} \right)\prime = \mathbf{B}\prime\mathbf{A}\prime.$



In general, matrix multiplication does not commute; that is, in general ***AB*** ≠ ***BA***, although there are some special cases in which matrix multiplication commutes; for example, if **`A`** and **`B`** are both $n \times n$ diagonal matrices, then ***AB*** = ***BA***.









# Matrix Inverse, Matrix Square Roots, and Related Topics







# The matrix inverse



Let **`A`** be a square matrix. Assuming that it exists, the inverse of the matrix **`A`** is defined as the matrix for which $\mathbf{A}^{- 1}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I}_{n}$. If, in, fact the inverse matrix **`A`**−1 exists, then **`A`** is said to be invertible or nonsingular. If both **`A`** and **`B`** are invertible, then ${(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})}^{- 1} = \mathbf{B}^{- 1}\mathbf{A}^{- 1}$.







# Positive definite and positive semidefinite matrices



Let **`V`** be an $n \times n$ square matrix. Then **`V`** is positive definite if $\mathbf{c}\prime\ \mathbf{V}\mathbf{c} > 0$ for all nonzero $n \times 1$ vectors **`c`**. Similarly, **`V`** is positive semidefinite if $\mathbf{c}\prime\ \mathbf{V}\mathbf{c} \geq 0$ for all nonzero $n \times 1$ vectors **`c`**. If **`V`** is positive definite, then it is invertible.







# Linear independence



The $n \times 1$ vectors **`a`**1 and **`a`**2 are linearly independent if there do not exist nonzero scalars `c`1 and `c`2 such that $c_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1} + c_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2} = 0_{\text{n} \times \text{1}}$. More generally, the set of `k` vectors $\mathbf{a}_{1},\,\mathbf{a}_{2},\cdots,\,\mathbf{a}_{k}$ is linearly independent if there do not exist nonzero scalars $c_{1},\, c_{2},\cdots,\, c_{k}$ such that $c_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1} + c_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2} + \,\cdots\, + c_{k}\mathbf{a}_{k} = 0_{n \times 1}$.







# The rank of a matrix



The rank of the $n \times m$ matrix **`A`** is the number of linearly independent columns of **`A`**. The rank of **`A`** is denoted rank(**`A`**). If the rank of **`A`** equals the number of columns of **`A`**, then **`A`** is said to have full column rank. If the $n \times m$ matrix **`A`** has full column rank, then there does not exist a nonzero $m \times 1$ vector **`c`** such that $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = 0_{n \times 1}$. If **`A`** is $n \times n$ with rank(**`A`**) = `n`, then **`A`** is nonsingular. If the $n \times m$ matrix **`A`** has full column rank, then $\mathbf{A}\prime\mathbf{A}$ is nonsingular.







# The trace of a matrix



The trace of the $n \times n$ (square) matrix **`A`** is the sum of the diagonal elements; that is, $\text{trace}\left( \mathbf{A} \right) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}a_{ii}$. For $n \times n$ matrices **`A`** and **`B`** and $n \times 1$ vector **`c`**, the trace satisfies these properties: trace(**`A`**) = trace(**`A`**'), trace(**`A`** + **`B`**) = trace(**`A`**) + trace(**`B`**), trace(***AB***) = trace(***BA***), trace(***BAB***−1) = trace(**`A`**), and **`c`**′ ***Bc*** = trace(***Bcc***′).







# The matrix square root



Let **`V`** be an $n \times n$ square symmetric positive definite matrix. The matrix square root of **`V`** is defined to be an $n \times n$ matrix **`F`** such that $\mathbf{F}\prime\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{V}$. The matrix square root of a positive definite matrix will always exist, but it is not unique. The matrix square root has the property that $\mathbf{F}\mathbf{V}^{- 1}\mathbf{F}\prime = \mathbf{I}_{n}$. In addition, the matrix square root of a positive definite matrix is invertible, so $\mathbf{F}\prime^{- 1}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{F}^{- 1} = \mathbf{I}_{n}.$







# Eigenvalues and eigenvectors



Let **`A`** be an $n \times n$ matrix. If the $n \times 1$ vector **`q`** and the scalar $\lambda$ satisfy $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q} = \lambda\mathbf{q}$, where $\mathbf{q}\prime\mathbf{q} = 1$, then $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of **`A`**, and **`q`** is the eigenvector of **`A`** associated with that eigenvalue. An $n \times n$ matrix has `n` eigenvalues, which need not take on distinct values, and `n` eigenvectors.

If **`V`** is an $n \times n$ symmetric positive definite matrix, then the eigenvalues of **`V`** are positive real numbers, and the eigenvectors of **`V`** are real. Also, **`V`** can be written in terms of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors as $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}\prime$, where $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ is a diagonal $n \times n$ matrix with diagonal elements that equal the eigenvalues of **`V`** and **`Q`** is an $n \times n$ matrix consisting of the eigenvectors of **`V`**, arranged so that the `i`th column of **`Q`** is the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{i}$, which is the `i`th diagonal element of $\mathbf{\Lambda}$. The eigenvectors are orthonormal, so $\mathbf{Q}\prime\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}_{n}.$ The trace of **`V`** equals the sum of its eigenvectors: $\text{trace}(\mathbf{V}) = \text{trace}(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}') = \text{trace}(\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}'\mathbf{Q}) = \text{trace}(\mathbf{\Lambda}) = {\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\lambda_{i}}$.







# Idempotent matrices



A matrix **`C`** is idempotent if **`C`** is square and $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}$. If **`C`** is an $n \times n$ idempotent matrix that is also symmetric, then **`C`** is positive semidefinite, and **`C`** has `r` eigenvalues that equal 1 and $n - r$ eigenvalues that equal 0, where $r = \text{rank}\left( \mathbf{C} \right)$ (Exercise 19.10).









<!--?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?-->





# Appendix 19.2 Multivariate Distributions



This appendix collects various definitions and facts about distributions of vectors of random variables. We start by defining the mean and covariance matrix of the `n`-dimensional random variable **`V`**. Next we present the multivariate normal distribution. Finally, we summarize some facts about the distributions of linear and quadratic functions of jointly normally distributed random variables.





# The Mean Vector and Covariance Matrix



The first and second moments of an $m \times 1$ vector of random variables, $\mathbf{V} = \left( {V_{1}\quad V_{2\ \quad}\cdots\quad V_{m}} \right)\prime\text{,}$ are summarized by its mean vector and covariance matrix.

Because **`V`** is a vector, the vector of its means—that is, its mean vector—is $E\left( \mathbf{V} \right) = \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}}$. The `i`th element of the mean vector is the mean of the `i`th element of **`V`**.

The covariance matrix of **`V`** is the matrix consisting of the variance ${var}(V_{i}),i = 1,\,\cdots,\, m$, along the diagonal and the (*i, j*) off-diagonal elements cov(`V``i`, `V``j`). In matrix form, the covariance matrix ***V*** is



$$\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}} = E\lbrack(\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}})(\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}})'\rbrack = \begin{bmatrix}
{{var}(V_{1})} & \cdots & {{cov}(V_{1},\, V_{m})} \\
 \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
{{cov}(V_{m},V_{1})} & \cdots & {{var}(V_{m})}
\end{bmatrix}.$$ (19.72)









# The Multivariate Normal Distribution



The $m \times 1$ vector random variable **`V`** has a multivariate normal distribution with mean vector $\mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}}$ and covariance matrix $\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}$ if it has the joint probability density function



$$f\left( \mathbf{V} \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\left( {2\pi} \right)^{m}\det\left( \textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}} \right)}}\exp\left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{2}\left( {\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}}} \right)^{- 1}\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}^{- 1}\left( {\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}}} \right)} \right\rbrack,$$ (19.73)



where $\text{det}\left( \textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}} \right)$ is the determinant of the matrix $\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}$. The multivariate normal distribution is denoted $N\left( {\mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}},\ \textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}} \right).$

An important fact about the multivariate normal distribution is that if two jointly normally distributed random variables are uncorrelated (or, equivalently, have a block-diagonal covariance matrix), then they are independently distributed. That is, let **`V`**1 and **`V`**2 be jointly normally distributed random variables with respective dimensions $m_{1} \times 1$ and $m_{2} \times 1$. Then if cov$\left( {\mathbf{V}_{1},\ \mathbf{V}_{2}} \right) = E\left\lbrack {\left( {\mathbf{V}_{1} - \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}_{1}}} \right)\left( {\mathbf{V}_{2} - \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}_{2}}} \right)\prime} \right\rbrack = 0_{m_{1} \times m_{2}},$ $\mathbf{V}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{V}_{2}$ are independent.

If {`V``i`} are i.i.d. $N(0,\,\sigma_{v}^{2})$, then $\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}} = \sigma_{v}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{m}$, and the multivariate normal distribution simplifies to the product of `m` univariate normal densities.







# Distributions of Linear Combinations and Quadratic Forms of Normal Random Variables



Linear combinations of multivariate normal random variables are themselves normally distributed, and certain quadratic forms of multivariate normal random variables have a chi-squared distribution. Let **`V`** be an $m \times 1$ random variable distributed $N\left( {\mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}},\ \textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}} \right)$, let **`A`** and **`B`** be nonrandom $a \times m$ and $b \times m$ matrices, and let **`d`** be a nonrandom $a \times 1$ vector. Then



$$\mathbf{d} + \mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\text{~is~distributed~}N\left( {\mathbf{d} + \mathbf{A}\mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}},\ \mathbf{A}\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{A}\prime} \right),\text{and}$$ (19.74)





$${\text{cov}\left( {\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V},\ \mathbf{B}\mathbf{V}\,} \right)} = \mathbf{A}\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{B}\prime;$$ (19.75)





$$\text{if~}\mathbf{A}\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{B}\prime = 0_{a \times b},\text{~then~}\textit{\textbf{AV}}\text{~and~}\textit{\textbf{BV}}\text{~are~independently~distributed;~and}$$ (19.76)





$$\left( {\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}}} \right)\prime\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}^{- 1}\left( {\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{\mu}_{\mathbf{V}}} \right)\text{~is~distributed~}\chi_{m}^{2}.$$ (19.77)



Let **`U`** be an `m`-dimensional multivariate standard normal random variable with distribution `N`(**0**, **`I`**<sub>`m`</sub>). If **`C`** is symmetric and idempotent, then



$$\mathbf{U}\prime\mathbf{C}\mathbf{U}\text{~has~a~}\chi_{r}^{2}\text{~distribution,~where~}r\ = \text{~rank}\left( \mathbf{C} \right).$$ (19.78)



Equation (19.78) is proven as Exercise 19.11.

# Appendix 19.3 Derivation of the Asymptotic Distribution of $\hat{\beta}$



This appendix provides the derivation of the asymptotic normal distribution of $\sqrt{n}\left( {\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{\beta}} \right)$ given in Equation (19.12). An implication of this result is that $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\mathbf{\beta}$.

First consider the “denominator” matrix ${{\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}}/n} = \frac{1}{n}{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{\mathbf{X}_{i}\mathbf{X}_{i}^{'}}}$ in Equation (19.15). The (`j`, `l`) element of this matrix is $\frac{1}{n}{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{X_{ij}X_{li}}}$. By the second assumption in Key Concept 19.1, **`X`**`i` is i.i.d., so *XjiXli* is i.i.d. By the third assumption in Key Concept 19.1, each element of **`X`**`i` has four moments, so, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Appendix 18.2), *XjiXli* has two moments. Because *XjiXli* is i.i.d. with two moments, $\frac{1}{n}{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{X_{ij}X_{li}}}$ obeys the law of large numbers, so $\frac{1}{n}{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{X_{ij}X_{li}}}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}E(X_{ji}X_{li})$. This is true for all the elements of $\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n$, so $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\mathbf{X}/n\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}E\left( {\mathbf{X}_{i}{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}}_{i}} \right) = \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}.$

Next consider the “numerator” matrix in Equation (19.15), ${{\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{U}}/{\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\mathbf{V}_{i}}}},$ where $\mathbf{V}_{i} = \mathbf{X}_{i}u_{i}$. By the first assumption in Key Concept 19.1 and the law of iterated expectations, $E\left( \mathbf{V}_{i} \right) = E\left\lbrack {\mathbf{X}_{i}E\left( {u_{i}|\mathbf{X}_{i}} \right)} \right\rbrack = 0_{k + 1}$. By the second least squares assumption, **`V`**`i` is i.i.d. Let **`c`** be a finite $k + 1$ dimensional vector. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $E\left\lbrack \left( {\mathbf{c}\prime\mathbf{V}_{i}} \right)^{2} \right\rbrack = E\left\lbrack \left( {\mathbf{c}\prime\mathbf{X}_{i}u_{i}} \right)^{2} \right\rbrack = E\left\lbrack {\left( {\mathbf{c}\prime\mathbf{X}_{i}} \right)^{2}\left( u_{i} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack\ \leq \ \sqrt{E\left\lbrack \left( {\mathbf{c}\prime\mathbf{X}_{i}} \right)^{4} \right\rbrack E\left( u_{i}^{4} \right)},$ which is finite by the third least squares assumption. This is true for every such vector **`c`**, so $E\left( {\mathbf{V}_{i}\mathbf{V}\prime_{i}} \right) = \textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}$ is finite and, we assume, positive definite. Thus the multivariate central limit theorem of Key Concept 19.2 applies to $\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\mathbf{V}_{i}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{U}$ that is,



$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{U}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}N(0_{k + 1},\,\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{V}}).$$ (19.79)



The result in Equation (19.12) follows from Equations (19.15) and (19.79), the consistency of $\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n,$ the fourth least squares assumption (which ensures that $\left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}$ exists), and Slutsky’s theorem.

# Appendix 19.4 Derivations of Exact Distributions of OLS Test Statistics with Normal Errors



This appendix presents the proofs of the distributions under the null hypothesis of the homoskedasticity-only `t`-statistic in Equation (19.35) and the homoskedasticity-only `F`-statistic in Equation (19.37), assuming that all six assumptions in Key Concept 19.1 hold.





# Proof of Equation (19.35)



If (i) `Z` has a standard normal distribution, (ii) `W` has a $\chi_{m}^{2}$ distribution, and (iii) `Z` and `W` are independently distributed, then the random variable $Z/\sqrt{W/m}$ has the `t` distribution with `m` degrees of freedom (Appendix 18.1). To put $\widetilde{t}$ in this form, notice that ${\hat{\textbf{Σ}}}_{\hat{\beta}} = ({s_{\hat{u}}^{2}/\sigma_{u}^{2}})\textbf{Σ}_{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}}.$ Then rewrite Equation (19.34) as



$$\widetilde{t} = \frac{{({{\hat{\beta}}_{j} - \beta_{j,0}})}/\sqrt{{(\textbf{Σ}_{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}})}_{jj}}}{\sqrt{W/{({n - k - 1})}}},$$ (19.80)



where $W = (n - k - 1)({s_{\hat{u}}^{2}/\sigma_{u}^{2}})$, and let $Z = {{({\hat{\beta}}_{j} - \beta_{j,0})}/\sqrt{{(\textit{\textbf{Σ}}_{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}\,|\,\mathbf{X}})}_{jj}}}$ and $m = n - k - 1$. With these definitions, $\widetilde{t} = {Z/\sqrt{W/m}}$. Thus, to prove the result in Equation (19.35), we must show (i) through (iii) for these definitions of `Z`, `W`, and `m`.

1.

An implication of Equation (19.30) is that, under the null hypothesis, $Z = {{(\hat{\beta} - \beta_{j,0})}/\sqrt{{(\textbf{Σ}_{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}\,|\,\mathbf{X}})}_{jj}}}$ has an exact standard normal distribution, which shows (i).



2.

From Equation (19.31), `W` is distributed as $\chi_{n - k - 1}^{2},$ which shows (ii).



3.

To show (iii), it must be shown that ${\hat{\beta}}_{j}$ and $s_{\hat{u}}^{2}$ are independently distributed.



From Equations (19.14) and (19.29), $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{\beta} = {({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{U}$ and $s_{\hat{u}}^{2} = {{(\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{U})'(\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{U})}/{(n - k - 1)}}$. Thus $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{\beta}$ and $s_{\hat{u}}^{2}$ are independent if ${({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{U}$ and ***MXU*** are independent. Both ${({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{U}$ and ***MXU*** are linear combinations of **`U`**, which has an $\mathbf{N}{({0_{n \times 1},\ \sigma_{u}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{n}})}$ distribution, conditional on **`X`**. But because $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{X}{({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1} = 0_{n \times {({k + 1})}}$ \[Equation (19.26)\], it follows that ${({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{U}$ and ***MXU*** are independently distributed \[Equation (19.76)\]. Consequently, under all six assumptions in Key Concept 19.1,



$${\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}\text{~and~}s_{\hat{u}}^{2}}\text{~are independently distributed},$$ (19.81)



which shows (iii) and thus proves Equation (19.35).







# Proof of Equation (19.37)



The $F_{n_{1},\ n_{2}}$ distribution is the distribution of ${({W_{1}/n_{1}})}/{({W_{2}/n_{2}})}$, where (i) `W`1 is distributed $\chi_{n_{1}}^{2}$; (ii) `W`2 is distributed $\chi_{n_{2}}^{2}$; and (iii) `W`1 and `W`2 are independently distributed (Appendix 18.1). To express $\widetilde{F}$ in this form, let $W_{1} = {({\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{r}})}\prime\left\lbrack {\mathbf{R}{({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{R}\prime\sigma_{u}^{2}} \right\rbrack^{- 1}{({\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - r})}$ and $W_{2} = {{(n - k - 1)s_{\hat{u}}^{2}}/\sigma_{u}^{2}}$. Substitution of these definitions into Equation (19.36) shows that $\widetilde{F} = {{({W_{1}/q})}/{\lbrack{W_{2}/{(n - k - 1)}}\rbrack}}.$ Thus, by the definition of the `F` distribution, $\widetilde{F}$ has an *Fq, n−k−*1 distribution if (i) through (iii) hold with $n_{1} = q$ and $n_{2} = n - k - 1$.

1.

Under the null hypothesis, $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{R}{({\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{\beta}})}$. Because $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}$ has the conditional normal distribution in Equation (19.30) and because **`R`** is a nonrandom matrix, $\mathbf{R}{({\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{\beta}})}$ is distributed $N{({0_{q \times 1},\ \mathbf{R}{({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{R}\prime\sigma_{u}^{2}})}\text{,}$ conditional on **`X`**. Thus, by Equation (19.77) in Appendix 19.2, ${({\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{r}})}\prime\left\lbrack {\mathbf{R}{({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}\mathbf{R}\prime\sigma_{u}^{2}} \right\rbrack^{- 1}{({\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - r})}$ is distributed $\chi_{q}^{2}$, proving (i).



2.

Requirement (ii) is shown in Equation (19.31).



3.

It has already been shown that $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{\beta}$ and $s_{\hat{u}}^{2}$ are independently distributed \[Equation (19.81)\]. It follows that $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} - \mathbf{r}$ and $s_{\hat{u}}^{2}$ are independently distributed, which in turn implies that `W`1 and `W`2 are independently distributed, proving (iii) and completing the proof.

# Appendix 19.5 Proof of the Gauss–Markov Theorem for Multiple Regression



This appendix proves the Gauss–Markov theorem (Key Concept 19.3) for the multiple regression model. Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}$ be a linear conditionally unbiased estimator of **`β`** so that $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}} = \mathbf{A}'\mathbf{Y}$ and $E(\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{\beta}$, where **`A`** is an $n \times (k + 1)$ matrix that can depend on **`X`** and nonrandom constants. We show that ${var}(\mathbf{c}'\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}) \leq {var}(\mathbf{c}'\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}})$ for all $k + 1$ dimensional vectors **`c`**, where the inequality holds with equality only if $\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}} = \hat{\mathbf{\beta}}$.

Because $\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}$ is linear, it can be written as $\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}} = \mathbf{A}'\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{A}'(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{U}) = (\mathbf{A}'\mathbf{X})\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{A}'\mathbf{U}.$ By the first Gauss–Markov condition, $E(\mathbf{U}|\mathbf{X}) = 0_{n \times 1}$, so $E(\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}) = (\mathbf{A}'\mathbf{X})\mathbf{\beta}$, but because $\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}$ is conditionally unbiased, $E\left( {\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}\mspace{2mu}|\mspace{2mu}\mathbf{X}} \right) = \mathbf{\beta} = \left( {\mathbf{A}\prime\mathbf{X}} \right)\mathbf{\beta},$ which implies that $\mathbf{A}\prime\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}_{k + 1}$. Thus $\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}} = \mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{A}\prime\mathbf{U}$, ${var}(\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}) = {var}(\mathbf{A}'\mathbf{U}|\mathbf{X}) = E(\mathbf{A}'\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}'\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{A}'E(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}'|\mathbf{X})\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{\sigma}_{u}^{2}\mathbf{A}'\mathbf{A}$, where the third equality follows because **`A`** can depend on **`X`** but not **`U`** and the final equality follows from the second Gauss–Markov condition. That is, if $\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}$ is linear and unbiased, then under the Gauss–Markov conditions,



$$\mathbf{A}\prime\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}_{k + 1}\text{~and~var}\left( {\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}} \right) = \sigma_{u}{}^{2\ }\mathbf{A}\prime\mathbf{A}.$$ (19.82)



The results in Equation (19.82) also apply to $\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}$ with $\mathbf{A} = \hat{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{X}\left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}$, where $\left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}$ exists by the third Gauss–Markov condition.

Now let $\mathbf{A} = \overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} + \mathbf{D}$, so that **`D`** is the difference between the matrices **`A`** and $\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}$. Note that $\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}\prime\mathbf{A} = {({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{A} = {({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}$ \[by Equation (19.82)\] and $\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}\prime\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} = {({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}{({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1} = {({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1},$ so $\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}\prime\mathbf{D} = \overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}\prime{({\mathbf{A} - \overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}})} = \overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}\prime\mathbf{A} - \overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}\prime\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} = 0_{{({k + \ 1})} \times {({k + \ 1})}}$. Substituting $\mathbf{A} = \overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} + \mathbf{D}$ into the formula for the conditional variance in Equation (19.82) yields



$$\begin{array}{lll}
{{var}(\overset{˜}{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X})} & = & {\sigma_{u}^{2}(\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} + \mathbf{D})'(\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} + \mathbf{D})} \\
 & = & {\sigma_{u}^{2}\lbrack\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}'\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} + \overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}'\mathbf{D} + \mathbf{D}'\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} + \mathbf{D}'\mathbf{D}\rbrack} \\
 & = & {\sigma_{u}^{2}{(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})}^{- 1} + \sigma_{u}^{2}\mathbf{D}'\mathbf{D},}
\end{array}$$ (19.83)



where the final equality uses the facts $\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}\prime\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}} = {({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}$ and $\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}'\mathbf{D} = 0_{(k + 1) \times (k + 1)}.$

Because $\text{var}{({\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{\beta}}\mspace{2mu}|\mspace{2mu}\mathbf{X}})} = \sigma_{u}^{2}{({\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1},$ Equations (19.82) and (19.83) imply that ${var}(\overset{˜}{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}) - {var}(\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}) = \sigma_{u}^{2}\mathbf{D}'\mathbf{D}$. The difference between the variances of the two estimators of the linear combination $\mathbf{c}\prime\mathbf{\beta}$ thus is



$${var}(\mathbf{c}'\overset{˜}{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}) - {var}(\mathbf{c}'\overset{˜}{\mathbf{\beta}}|\mathbf{X}) = \sigma_{u}^{2}\mathbf{c}'\mathbf{D}'\mathbf{D}\mathbf{c} \geq 0.$$ (19.84)



The inequality in Equation (19.84) holds for all linear combinations $\mathbf{c}\prime\mathbf{\beta}$, and the inequality holds with equality for all nonzero **`c`** only if $\mathbf{D} = 0_{n \times (k + 1)}$—that is, if $\mathbf{A} = \overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{A}}$ or, equivalently, `β`. Thus $\mathbf{c}\prime\overset{\hat{}}{\mathbf{\beta}}$ has the smallest variance of all linear conditionally unbiased estimators of $\mathbf{c}\prime\mathbf{\beta}$; that is, the OLS estimator is BLUE.

# Appendix 19.6 Proof of Selected Results for IV and GMM Estimation







# The Efficiency of TSLS Under Homoskedasticity \[Proof of Equation (19.62)\]



When the errors `u``i` are homoskedastic, the difference between $\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV}$ \[Equation (19.61)\] and $\textbf{Σ}^{TSLS}$ \[Equation (19.55)\] is given by



$$\begin{matrix}
{\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV} - \textbf{Σ}^{TSLS} = \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\sigma_{u}^{2} - \left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\sigma_{u}^{2}} \\
{\text{~~} = {(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\lbrack\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}} - \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}{(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\rbrack\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}{(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\sigma_{u}^{2},}
\end{matrix}$$ (19.85)



where the second term within the brackets in the second equality follows from $\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{I}_{({k + \ r + \ 1})}$. Let **`F`** be the matrix square root of ***QZZ***, so $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}} = \mathbf{F}\prime\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1} = \mathbf{F}^{- 1}\mathbf{F}^{- 1\prime}$. \[The latter equality follows from noting that $\left( {\mathbf{F}\prime\mathbf{F}} \right)^{- 1} = \mathbf{F}^{- 1}\mathbf{F}\prime^{- 1}$ and $\mathbf{F}\prime^{- 1} = \mathbf{F}^{- 1\prime}$.\] Then the final expression in Equation (19.85) can be rewritten to yield



$$\begin{array}{ccl}
{\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV} - \textbf{Σ}^{TSLS}} & = & {\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{F}\prime\left\lbrack {I - \mathbf{F}^{- 1\prime}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{F}^{- 1}\mathbf{F}^{- 1\prime}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{F}^{- 1}} \right\rbrack} \\
 & & {\times \mathbf{F}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}{(\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}})}^{- 1}\sigma_{u}^{2},}
\end{array}$$ (19.86)



where the second expression within the brackets uses $\mathbf{F}\prime\mathbf{F}^{- 1\prime} = \mathbf{I}$. Thus



$$\mathbf{c}\prime\left( {\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV} - \textbf{Σ}^{TSLS}} \right)\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{d}\prime\left\lbrack {\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}\left( {\mathbf{D}\prime\mathbf{D}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{D}\prime} \right\rbrack\mathbf{d}\sigma_{u}^{2},$$ (19.87)



where $\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1\,}\mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{F}^{- 1\prime}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}$. Now $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}\left( {\mathbf{D}\prime\mathbf{D}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{D}\prime$ is a symmetric idempotent matrix (Exercise 19.5). As a result, $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}\left( {\mathbf{D}\prime\mathbf{D}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{D}\prime$ has eigenvalues that are either 0 or 1, and $\mathbf{d}\prime\left\lbrack {\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}\left( {\mathbf{D}\prime\mathbf{D}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{D}\prime} \right\rbrack\mathbf{d} \geq 0$ (Exercise 19.10). Thus $\mathbf{c}\prime\left( {\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV} - \textbf{Σ}^{TSLS}} \right)\mathbf{c} \geq 0,$ proving that TSLS is efficient under homoskedasticity.







# Asymptotic Distribution of the `J`-Statistic Under Homoskedasticity



The `J`-statistic is defined in Equation (19.63). First note that



$$\begin{array}{lll}
\hat{\mathbf{U}} & = & {\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}{\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{TSLS}} \\
 & = & {\mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{X}{(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Y}} \\
 & = & {(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{U}) - \mathbf{X}{(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta} + \mathbf{U})} \\
 & = & {\mathbf{U} - \mathbf{X}{(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{U}} \\
 & = & {\lbrack\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{X}{(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\rbrack\mathbf{U}.}
\end{array}$$ (19.88)



Thus



$$\begin{array}{lll}
{\hat{\mathbf{U}}\,\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}} & = & {\mathbf{U}\prime\left\lbrack {\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X}\left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime} \right\rbrack\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{X}\left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{U}} \\
 & = & {\mathbf{U}'\lbrack\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}} - \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X}{(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{X})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\rbrack\mathbf{U},}
\end{array}$$ (19.89)



where the second equality follows by simplifying the preceding expression. Because $\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}$ is symmetric and positive definite, it can be written in terms of its matrix square root, $\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z} = \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2\prime}\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2},$ and this matrix square root is invertible, so $\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1} = \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2\prime},$ where $\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2} = \left\lbrack \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2} \right\rbrack^{- 1}$. Thus ***PZ*** can be written as $\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}} = \mathbf{Z}\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Z}\prime = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}\prime$ where $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{Z}\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}$. Substituting this expression for ***PZ*** into the final expression in Equation (19.89) yields



$$\begin{array}{lll}
{\hat{\mathbf{U}}'\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}} & = & {\mathbf{U}'\lbrack\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}' - \mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}'\mathbf{X}{(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}'\mathbf{X})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}'\rbrack\mathbf{U}} \\
 & = & {\mathbf{U}'\mathbf{B}\lbrack\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{B}'\mathbf{X}{(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}'\mathbf{X})}^{- 1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{B}\rbrack\mathbf{B}'\mathbf{U}} \\
 & = & {\mathbf{U}'\mathbf{B}\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{B}'\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{B}'\mathbf{U},}
\end{array}$$ (19.90)



where $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{B}\prime\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{B}\prime\mathbf{X}\left( {\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}\prime\mathbf{X}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{B}$ is a symmetric idempotent matrix.

The asymptotic null distribution of $\hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ is found by computing the limits in probability and in distribution of the various terms in the final expression in Equation (19.90) under the null hypothesis. Under the null hypothesis that $E\left( {\mathbf{Z}_{i}u_{i}} \right) = 0,\ \mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{U}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu}\sqrt{n}$ has mean 0, and the central limit theorem applies, so $\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{U}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu}\sqrt{n}\ \operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\ N\left( {0,\ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\sigma_{u}^{2}} \right)$. In addition, $\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n\ \operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}$ and $\mathbf{X}\prime\mathbf{Z}\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} n\ \operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}$. Thus $\mathbf{B}\prime\mathbf{U}\ = \ \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}} \right)^{- 1/2\prime}\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{U}\ = \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}/n} \right)^{- 1/2\prime}\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{U}/\sqrt{n}} \right)\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\sigma_{u}z$, where **`z`** is distributed $N\left( {0_{m + r + 1},\ \mathbf{I}_{m + r + 1}} \right)$. In addition, $\mathbf{B}\prime\mathbf{X}\mspace{2mu}/\sqrt{n} = \left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{Z}/n} \right)^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2\prime}\left( {\mathbf{Z}\prime\mathbf{X}/\mspace{2mu} n} \right)\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}},$ so $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{B}\prime\mathbf{X}}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}\ }^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}\left( {\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}\ }\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}{}_{\text{~~}}^{\prime}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}{}^{\prime} = \mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}}.$ Thus



$$\hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\left( {\mathbf{z}\prime\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{{- 1}/2}\ }\mathbf{z}} \right)\sigma_{u}^{2}.$$ (19.91)



Under the null hypothesis, the TSLS estimator is consistent, and the coefficients in the regression of $\hat{\mathbf{U}}$ on **`Z`** converge in probability to 0 \[an implication of Equation (19.91)\], so the denominator in the definition of the `J`-statistic is a consistent estimator of $\sigma_{u}^{2}$:



$$\hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}/\left( {n - m - r - 1} \right)\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{p}\sigma_{u}^{2}.$$ (19.92)



From the definition of the `J`-statistic and Equations (19.91) and (19.92), it follows that



$$\mathbf{J} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}}{\hat{\mathbf{U}}\prime\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{Z}}\hat{\mathbf{U}}/\left( {n - m - r - 1} \right)}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\mathbf{z}\prime\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1/2}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Z}}}\mathbf{z}.$$ (19.93)



Because **`z`** is a standard normal random vector and $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}}$ is a symmetric idempotent matrix, **`J`** is distributed as a chi-squared random variable with degrees of freedom that equals the rank of $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}}$ \[Equation (19.78)\]. Because $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}$ is $\left( {m + r + 1} \right) \times \left( {k + r + 1} \right)$ and `m` \> `k`, the rank of $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}^{- 1\mspace{2mu}/\mspace{2mu} 2}\ \mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{X}}}$ is `m` − `k` \[Exercise 19.5\]. Thus $\mathbf{J}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\chi_{m - k}^{2}$, which is the result stated in Equation (19.64).







# The Efficiency of the Efficient GMM Estimator



The infeasible efficient GMM estimator, ${\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$, is defined in Equation (19.66). The proof that ${\widetilde{\mathbf{\beta}}}^{Eff.GMM}$ is efficient entails showing that $\mathbf{c}\prime\left( {\textbf{Σ}_{\mathbf{A}}^{IV} - \textbf{Σ}^{Eff.GMM}} \right)\mathbf{c} \geq 0$ for all vectors **`c`**. The proof closely parallels the proof of the efficiency of the TSLS estimator in the first section of this appendix, with the sole modification that **`H`**−1 replaces $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{Z}}\sigma_{u}^{2}$ in Equation (19.85) and subsequently.







# Distribution of the GMM `J`-Statistic



The GMM `J`-statistic is given in Equation (19.70). The proof that, under the null hypothesis, $J^{GMM}\operatorname{\& xrarr;}\limits^{d}\chi_{m - k}^{2}$ closely parallels the corresponding proof for the TSLS `J`-statistic under homoskedasticity.
